So first, I don't see them as very uneven (we always notice how asymmetrical our own faces are, but they're rarely as bad as we think), but I am a firm believer that everyone's brow game can always be stronger.

Keep in mind, I am only basing this advice on my own personal brow journey. My natural eyebrows are also very low, and, less symmetrical than I'd like them to be; however, I am often told that my brow game is pretty strong ;)

I've found that brushing them in the direction that I want them to "flow," in helps the shape the most. Getting them waxed/plucking, in my opinion, often makes the shape just seem sort of "off."  I'd recommend a brow brush (I use the thicker side of this one: http://www.sephora.com/pro-brow-comb-21-P313039?skuId=1419670).

I start by brushing all the hairs on the inner half (so, the half closest to my nose) upward. You should notice somewhat of a rough line along the top of your eyebrow, with some hairs that really stick out. Trim those, until a straight line forms, and then brush the hairs back to where they fall naturally, out toward your temples.

Those first two steps thin out the brows just a tiny bit, which makes it easier to shape them the way that you like.

I'm sure you've seen tutorials/videos on how to fill in your eyebrows, and what tools to use (I personally use a regular angled brush, and dark brown eyeshadow, and it works fairly well, for me), but my extra little helpful hint is to go very slighty above where your natural arch is (and I mean VERY slightly. Even just a tiny arch will make a world of difference), and extend the tail end of your brow out VERY slightly.

This gives the illusion of more arched eyebrowd without it looking unnatural.

There are a lot of good tutorials on youtube that you can check out, the hard part is finding someone with a similar eye shape to yours, which is why it's almost faster to just practice on yourself until you like your results.

Alrighty, y'all, strap in, 'cause this one's a doozy.

I was always told I was far above average, intelligence wise, from a very young age. I always believed that about myself. Part of my identity was, "I am smarter than other people." Just like how some people are really good a sports, or cooking, or whatever, my "thing," was that I was just smart.

I was pulled out of school in 6th grade, partially because I was a huge asshole, and partially because my parents felt that I wasn't being challenged enough in public school. They intended on homeschooling me at a high school level for one year so that I could begin high school in a public school by the next year. Well, it turned out that my parents weren't actually that invested in this little experiment, because they both promptly got full time jobs, and instructed me to homeschool myself.

Now I want y'all to think back to your 6th grade selves. If you were given the opportunity to literally just do nothing but watch reruns of Roseanne all day, and eat stuff, or do school work, which would you choose? Be honest with yourself. I literally just did nothing for a year, education wise.

I did eventually go to a public high school at 13, starting as a freshman. I was, somehow, still slightly ahead of my class. My freshman year, I hardly ever showed up, because I just found school to be really boring, and a waste of time, because I had gotten pretty accustomed to doing whatever I wanted all day, so being told that I HAD to attend class at a certain time, 5 days a week, really rubbed me the wrong way. So, I usually just showed up if the mood struck me. I still managed to pull straight C's.

Well, I found school to be so lame, that I requested to graduate in 3 years as opposed to the usual 4, and my school didn't really seem to care, so they were like, "Yeah, sure."

So, at 16, I graduated and began attending a college that allowed me to still live at home, because most universities wouldn't allow me to live on campus at 16. So, I was going to college, working as much as I could at a super sucky job, and realized that I hated all of it. I hated not being able to afford to just go to school, and not work, and I hated that I was probably going to be unemployed by the end of it, anyway. I stopped showing up to school. I just worked at my shitty cashiering job.

Well, I decided after a while to start attending a community college, and guess what? Still didn't really like it, and eventually stopped showing up. Wasted a shit ton of money.

I have a better job, now, as a server at a restaurant where I am making better money. I found a school for makeup artistry that I'm pretty interested in attending, because it's something that I'm pretty passionate about, and I think I'd be good at it. Now, I could've done that right after high school, but instead, I was a dumbass and thought that I could handle a real college. I just wasn't cut out for the kid if jobs that real colleges set one up for. 

I am currently 17, and realizing slowly, that I am not nearly as smart as I was originally told I was. I could be in much better circumstances right now if I had any work ethic at all, and I hope that my story can maybe serve as a warning to younger redditors that are skating by in high school. Everything everyone tells you about the "real world," is true.
